description: We are a pair of highly motivated individuals, ready to deliver a beautiful VR experience to tackle this challenge.
summary: We created a Mars field trip that you can experience in a VR headset or your regular web browser. It renders the plains of the craters delta at real scale from images and terrain data obtained by NASA's satellites and superimposes what is really there, the real route of perseverance, the real locations of its sealed sample tubes, and an orbital mineral map. You spawn inside a rover cabin and need to choose three deposits to examine.Then, the system maps out a route that steers clear of slopes steeper than 15° and out you go, with an EVA clock ticking down the clock. The route has four stops: check out the slope dangers yourself, trace the rover tracks, press a drill into the simulated core where Perseverance extracted a real one, and stand inside the rover's panoramas. A handheld tablet on your forearm turns each data layer on and off, and each data card identifies which NASA dataset it originated from. Our map gathers together NASA data that is usually isolated in its own silos and makes it human scale so that you experience how the landscape, time and scientific objectives shape your walk across the surface.
details:
Project overview

Marswalk is an interactive 3D prototype for planning a science-focused surface mission in Jezero crater. It combines Mars terrain, imagery, rover information, and mineral data in a walkable, true-scale environment. Users can explore on a desktop or enter VR.

How it works

The mission begins in a simulated rover cabin, where the explorer reviews a map and selects three mineral targets from candidate deposits. Marswalk then replans the route to include those targets and guides the explorer through science stops. Along the way, users can inspect terrain slopes, Perseverance’s rover traverse, sample locations, and surface panoramas. A tablet and helmet-style HUD display the route, next stop, heading, slope, and estimated time to return. Users can collect simulated samples, return to the rover, and review a mission debrief.

The route planner uses A* search across a 2-meter terrain grid. Its 15-degree slope limit and mission-time calculations are team assumptions, clearly identified in the project.

Data and tools

Marswalk uses HiRISE imagery and terrain products for Jezero, Perseverance traverse and waypoint data, NASA sample information and Navcam panoramas, and an approximate mineral layer based on CRISM spectral data. The mineral layer has 36-meter pixels and shows possible mineral matches, not hazards.

The project was built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Three.js, and WebXR, with Python and Node.js tools for preparing data and routes. It is designed for browser-based VR, meaning all you have to do is load the website onto a browser in a headset to enter the VR experience, but you can also try it out through a regular desktop computer.

Benefits and intended impact

Marswalk brings imagery, terrain, rover information, and mineral data together in one local view. This helps users connect scientific targets with the ground they would cross to reach them. Explorers can compare direct and planned routes, see slope information, consider how target choices affect a route, and review estimated time to return. The interactive 3D and VR experience can also help students and the public better understand the challenges of exploring Mars.

Marswalk is a planning and learning prototype. Its route and time estimates use team assumptions, mineral identifications are approximate, and sample collection is simulated. It is not validated for real astronaut operations.

Creativity and factors considered

Marswalk combines a walkable 3D terrain map with a mission experience: a rover cabin briefing, selectable science targets, route replanning, an explorer tablet, a helmet-style HUD, sample collection, and a debrief. We considered astronaut safety, terrain slope, time to return, scientific value, and the limits of the available data. This is not a technically validated system for real astronaut operations, but given the opportunity to work with real NASA scientists, we can definitely create a validated tool that is useful to real astronauts.

Future work

We hope to expand Marswalk to other points of interest on Mars, including locations studied by other rover and orbital missions. This would let users explore different landscapes, compare science targets, and plan new mission routes using available data for each site. We also hope to add more data layers and improve the experience based on testing and user feedback, and potentially work with real NASA scientists to improve the tool's accuracy.
